title: Eviction hysteresis and tail-latency under mixed workloads - field notes
content:
Overview:

This doc captures exploratory notes and results from a set of experiments that evaluate how adding eviction hysteresis (temporal holdoffs and soft-TTLs) affects tail latencies (p95/p99) under mixed inference workloads. The motivating problem: when the KV cache is small relative to a multi-tenant hotset, eviction oscillations and aggressive immediate-evict policies produce periodic page-ins and memory-bandwidth spikes that correlate with long tail token latencies. We traded off reuse rate and steady-state occupancy against tail latency.

Goals:
- Quantify impact of different hysteresis strategies (time-based holdoff, reuse-count grace window, soft-TTL) on p95/p99 token latency for mixed workloads.
- Measure memory-bandwidth and page fault activity during eviction waves.
- Identify sweet spots where small increases in steady-state occupancy reduce long-tail latencies without unacceptable unit-cost increases.
- Surface any NUMA/PCIe transfer amplification when hysteresis increases residency.

Hypotheses tested:
1) Short hysteresis (e.g., 50-200 ms holdoff after load) reduces eviction churn and lowers p99 spikes, at the cost of small occupancy increase.
2) Long hysteresis (>1s) increases average memory footprint enough to saturate DRAM channels under bursty arrival patterns, creating new long tails from bandwidth queuing.
3) Reuse-count based grace windows (keep entry for N next-seen tokens) better align with real request patterns than fixed time TTLs.

Testbed and configs:
- Machines: r-inf-gpu-8 (8xA100-like emulated), 2xNUMA domains. OS: Ubuntu 22.04. Kernel: 6.1.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@feature/eviction-hysteresis (PR 987). Binaries instrumented with perf-events and custom telemetry hooks.
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes derived from production traces (sampled anonymized):
  * Search-heavy (SH): short contexts, high QPS, high repeated prefixes (good reuse).
  * Long-conversation (LC): long contexts, low QPS, high KV working set per session.
  * Mixed-burst (MB): 70% SH + 30% LC skewed bursts to simulate multi-tenant.
- Cache sizes: 4GB, 8GB, 16GB (representative of different instance classes).
- Eviction policies compared: LRU baseline (immediate evict), LRU+time-hysteresis (hold 100ms / 500ms / 2000ms), LRU+reuse-count (grace window of 2/5/10 hits), soft-TTL (entry age soft-fade with priority).
- Metrics captured: token p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, reuse rate (fraction of requests served from KV), eviction rate (entries/sec), page-fault rate (minor/major), DRAM bandwidth (via perf or ipmctl), CPU steal and PCIe transfers, GC/compaction pauses.

Methodology notes:
- For each config we run 30-minute steady-state runs with a 5 minute ramp. Each run repeated 3x.
- Telemetry: token latency traced by request id, eviction events annotated with resident-size and age.
- Perf counters: 'mem_load_uops_retired.l1_miss', 'LLC-load-misses', 'uncore_imc_data_read' (where available) to estimate DRAM bytes. We cross-validated with node-level bandwidth tools (intel pcm / ipmctl).
- NUMA: pinned and unpinned runs to measure cross-node eviction amplification.

Key findings (summary):
1) Short hysteresis (100-200ms) consistently reduced p99 token latency by 18-32% on MB workload at 8GB cache size, while increasing occupancy by 6-12%. Reuse rate rose by 5-10%. Eviction rate decreased ~25%.
2) At 2s hysteresis the system saw discoordination between eviction and prefetch; on MB workload DRAM bandwidth utilization climbed from 58% -> 83% and p99 increased beyond baseline (regression). This supports hypothesis #2.
3) Reuse-count grace window of 5 hits produced the best p95/p99 tradeoff for LC workload: it kept long-session state alive without sustaining large cold prefixes for unrelated tenants.
4) Soft-TTL produced smoother eviction curves but was sensitive to tuning; misconfigured half-life produced either premature evictions or long-lived garbage.
5) NUMA cross-node effects: with hysteresis enabled, we observed more frequent remote-page reads when the node-local eviction policy held entries past local memory pressure. In one run (MB / 8GB / 500ms hold) remote DRAM reads increased 3x vs baseline and p99 saw secondary spikes tied to PCIe/NUMA transfer stalls.

Representative numbers (MB, 8GB cache):
- Baseline LRU immediate-evict: p95=210ms, p99=720ms, reuse_rate=42%, eviction_rate=9200/s, DRAM bw avg=58%
- LRU + 100ms hold: p95=190ms, p99=510ms, reuse_rate=47%, eviction_rate=6900/s, DRAM bw avg=63%
- LRU + 500ms hold: p95=200ms, p99=480ms, reuse_rate=50%, eviction_rate=5200/s, DRAM bw avg=71%
- LRU + 2000ms hold: p95=230ms, p99=980ms, reuse_rate=62%, eviction_rate=1200/s, DRAM bw avg=83% (regression)

Observations and root causes:
- Eviction oscillations: immediate-evict LRU causes frequent churn when hotset size slightly exceeds cache. Churn correlates to bursts of page-fault handling and KV reloads; these create p99 spikes. Hysteresis dampens oscillation but transfers the load from eviction spikes to sustained bandwidth pressure.
- Bandwidth queuing: when many entries are kept longer, background prefetch/populate operations compete with on-path token generation memory accesses; the high-bandwidth prefetch can increase DRAM read latencies and exacerbate tail latency.
- NUMA remote-access amplification: hysteresis increased the probability that an entry live on the remote node will be accessed while local memory is pressured; remote reads (or migrations) add tens-to-hundreds of microseconds per access and manifest at token-level tail.
- Reuse-count advantages: counting real uses aligns with application patterns more directly than time windows; it avoids holding cold entries just because of transient spike in requests.

Practical recommendations (for product/ops):
1) Default: enable short time-hysteresis (100–300ms) on multi-tenant smaller instances (<=8GB) to reduce p99 spikes for typical mixed workloads.
2) Add adaptive hysteresis rule: increase holdoff when eviction churn metric > threshold AND DRAM bandwidth < 70%; if bandwidth > 75% automatically backoff hysteresis. This keeps a safety valve to avoid bandwidth saturation.
3) Prefer reuse-count = 3–6 for long-session modes (LC) where repeated access pattern is common.
4) Add NUMA-aware eviction: prefer evicting remote-resident entries first when local contention is high, or bias hysteresis to local pages only.
5) Expose telemetry & alerting: eviction_churn (evicts/s), host_dram_bandwidth_pct, remote_reads/s, and a hysteresis_backoff_flag. Add an alert when hysteresis is active and host_dram_bandwidth_pct > 80%.
6) Run a controlled canary with hysteresis enabled across Dedicated pools (small fraction) for two weeks; collect p99 and bandwidth signals.

Open questions / next experiments:
- More granular telemetry to correlate per-token micro-latency to specific eviction/populate RPC timings.
- Evaluate hybrid strategy: reuse-count + tiny time-hold (e.g., 2 hits OR 100ms whichever first).
- Test with larger real-world workloads (customer A's trace) with longer session skew to validate reuse-count heuristics.
- Quantify cost impact (tokens per dollar) from occupancy increase across instance classes.

Action items:
- [Aisha] Wire adaptive hysteresis POC (feature/auto-hysteresis branch) and implement bandwidth-sensing backoff (due 2025-03-10). Linked PR: PR 987 in Github.
- [Connor] Build dashboard for eviction_churn / dram_bw / remote_reads and add alert rule (INF-321).
- [Marisol] Run canary on dedicated-small pool and collect 2 weeks of p50/p95/p99 and occupancy numbers (start 2025-03-15).

Quick notes / anecdotal traces:
- Slack: thread #serving-runtime: 'noticed >10x p99 after midday burst' (ts 2025-02-25) maps to one run where hysteresis was misconfigured to 3s.
- Perf snippet that was useful: perf stat -I 1000 -e LLC-load-misses,mem_load_uops_retired.l1_miss,cycles -a to observe instantaneous miss trends aligned to p99 spikes.

Conclusion:
Short hysteresis is a low-risk, high-reward tuning knob for reducing tail latencies with modest occupancy cost. However, hysteresis must be adaptive and NUMA-aware to avoid creating a new failure mode from sustained DRAM bandwidth pressure and remote-read amplification. The next step is to prototype the adaptive backoff and run a small production canary to validate in the wild.

Notes for doc consumers: this is exploratory field notes and not yet a final runbook. See linked PR and Linear ticket for implementation details and follow-up tasks.
